(p-6) Regarding ﴿Indeed the Word has come true﴾, there are two opinions. The first: the punishment became due. The second: the Word had already decreed their disbelief.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿upon most of them﴾, means the people of Makkah. This points to Allah's prior will regarding their disbelief. ﴿So they do not believe﴾ because of the decree (qadar) that had already preceded concerning this.

Regarding ﴿We have put shackles upon their necks﴾, there are three opinions.

The first: it is a parable (mathal, an illustrative image), and there is no actual shackle. This is the view of most of the careful scholars (al-muhaqqiqun). Within this view there are three opinions. The first is that it is a parable for their being prevented from every good. This was said by Qatadah. The second is that it is a parable for their being held back from spending in the way of Allah by barriers like shackles. This was said by al-Farra' and Ibn Qutaybah. (p-6) Regarding ﴿Indeed the Word has come true﴾, there are two opinions. The first: the punishment became due. The second: the Word had already decreed their disbelief.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿upon most of them﴾, means the people of Makkah. This points to Allah's prior will regarding their disbelief. ﴿So they do not believe﴾ because of the decree (qadar) that had already preceded concerning this.

Within this view there are three opinions. The first is that it is a parable for their being prevented from every good. This was said by Qatadah. The second is that it is a parable for their being held back from spending in the way of Allah by barriers like shackles. This was said by al-Farra' and Ibn Qutaybah. The third is that it is a parable for their being prevented from believing in Allah. This was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

The second opinion: they are literal physical barriers that hindered them as a shackle hinders. Muqatil ibn Sulayman said: "Abu Jahl swore that if he saw the Prophet ﷺ praying, he would crush him. So he came to him while he was praying, and he raised a rock, but his hand dried up and the rock stuck to his hand. He returned to his companions and informed them of the matter. Then a man from among them stood up and took the rock, but when he approached the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, Allah blinded his sight so he did not see him. He returned to his companions and did not perceive them until they called out to him." (p-7) The third opinion: it is to be taken literally, but it is a description of what Allah will send upon them in the Fire. This was related by al-Mawardi.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿so they are up to the chins﴾. al-Farra' said: "fa-hiya" is a kinaya (a pronoun referring to something implied but not mentioned), referring to the hands, and it is not mentioned because a shackle is only on the right hand and the neck together, so mention of one of them suffices over the other. al-Zajjaj said: "hiya" refers to the hands, and it is not mentioned for brevity, because the shackle includes the hand and the neck. He recited:

؎ And I do not know, when I set out toward a land seeking good, which of the two will restrain me.

He only said "ayyuhuma" (which of the two) because he knew that good and evil are presented to a person.

Ibn Qutaybah said: it is said, "ba'ir qamih" (a camel that is qamih) and "ibil qimah" when they have drunk water and raised their heads (qamahat). The poet said, describing a ship:

؎ And we are sitting on its sides, lowering our gaze like thirsty camels that have raised their heads.

al-Azhari said: The meaning is that when their hands were shackled at their necks, the shackles raised their chins and heads, so they are raised-headed because the shackles raise them.

﴿When We sent to them two﴾. There are three opinions concerning their names. The first: Sadiq and Saduq, said by Ibn ʿAbbas and Kaʿb. The second: Yuhanna and Bulus, said by Wahb ibn Munabbih. The third: Tuman and Bulus, said by Muqatil.

(p-11) His words, exalted is He: ﴿So We strengthened [fa-ʿazzaznā]﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafiʿ, Abu ʿAmr, Ibn ʿAmir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs on the authority of ʿAsim read "fa-ʿazzaznā" with the zay doubled (shaddah). Ibn Qutaybah said: the meaning is "We strengthened and reinforced," as it is said, "taʿazzaza laḥmu al-nāqah," meaning the camel's meat became firm when it hardened. Abu Bakr and al-Mufaddal on the authority of ʿAsim read "fa-ʿazaznā" with a single (light) zay. Abu ʿAli said: he intended "fa-ghalabnā," "so We overpowered." (p-12) What follows is clear up to His words: ﴿They said, "Indeed we consider you a bad omen"﴾. That is because rain was withheld from them, so they said, "This has only befallen us because of you." ﴿If you do not desist﴾: that is, if you do not keep silent about us. ﴿We will surely stone you﴾: that is, we will surely kill you.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 36, verses 20–29:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And there came from the farthest part of the city a man, running﴾. His name was Habib the carpenter (Habib al-Najjar). He had leprosy, and he had believed in the messengers when they arrived at the town. His dwelling was near the farthest gate of the town. When it reached him that his people had denied the messengers and intended to kill them, he came running, and he said what Allah related to us, up to His saying: ﴿and they are guided﴾, meaning the messengers. They seized him and brought him to the king. The king said to him: "Do you follow them?" He said: ﴿And what is it for me﴾ (Hamzah, Khalaf and Ya'qub pronounced the final yā' of wa-mā lī as a sukun), ﴿that I should not worship He who created me﴾, meaning: "What is it for me if I do not worship my Creator?" ﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾ at the Resurrection, so that He will recompense you for your disbelief?!

If it is asked: Why did he attribute the creation (fitrah) to himself and the return to them, when he knows that Allah created them all just as He will resurrect them all?

The answer: Allah's bringing a thing into existence is a blessing that necessitates gratitude, while the resurrection on the Day of Resurrection is a warning that necessitates deterrence. So attributing the blessing to himself was more apparent in gratitude, and attributing the resurrection to the disbeliever was more forceful in deterrence.

Then he denied the worship of idols by his saying: ﴿Shall I take besides Him gods?﴾

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Their intercession will not avail me at all﴾, meaning there is no intercession for them that would benefit. ﴿Nor can they save me﴾. Ya'qub and Warsh affirmed the yā' in both states here. The meaning: they cannot rescue me from that harm. ﴿Indeed I would then be in clear error﴾: Nafi' and Abu 'Amr opened (fatḥah) this yā'.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed I have believed in your Lord﴾: Ahl al-Hijaz and Abu 'Amr opened this yā'.

Regarding whom he addressed with his faith, there are two opinions. One: he addressed his people with that; this was said by Ibn Mas'ud. The second: he addressed the messengers.

The meaning of ﴿so listen to me﴾ is: bear witness for me in this, as said by al-Farra'. Abu 'Ubaydah said: the meaning is: so listen to me. Ya'qub affirmed the yā' in "fasma'ūnī" in both states. Ibn Mas'ud said: when he addressed his people with that, they trampled him with their feet. al-Suddi said: they pelted him with stones while he was saying: "O Allah, guide my people."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿It was said: Enter Paradise﴾. When they killed him and he met Allah, it was said to him: "Enter Paradise." (p-14) When he entered it, ﴿he said: Would that my people knew﴾ ﴿of how my Lord has forgiven me﴾. Regarding "mā" there are two opinions.

One: it, together with "ghafara" (forgave), is in the position of a verbal noun; the meaning is: by the forgiveness of Allah to me.

The second: it means "alladhī" (that which); the meaning is: would that they knew of that by which my Lord forgave me, so that they would believe. Thus he advised them while alive and dead.

When they killed him, Allah hastened the punishment upon them. This is His saying: ﴿And We did not send down upon his people﴾, meaning the people of Habib, ﴿after him﴾, that is, after his killing, ﴿any host from the heaven﴾, meaning the angels; that is, He did not take vengeance upon them with a host from the heaven. ﴿Nor was it [Our practice] that We would send them down﴾ upon nations when We destroy them. It was also said: the meaning is: We did not send after him any prophet to them, nor did We send down to them any message.

﴿It was but one shout﴾. The commentators said: Jibril (Gabriel), peace be upon him, took hold of the two posts of the gate of the town, then shouted at them one shout, and behold, they were dead, with no sound heard from them, like a fire when it is extinguished. This is His saying: ﴿and behold, they were extinguished﴾, meaning: still, like the state of extinguished ashes.

So attributing the blessing to himself was more apparent in gratitude, and attributing the resurrection to the disbeliever was more forceful in deterrence.

Then he denied the worship of idols by his saying: ﴿Shall I take besides Him gods?﴾

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Their intercession will not avail me at all﴾, meaning there is no intercession for them that would benefit. ﴿Nor can they save me﴾. Ya'qub and Warsh affirmed the yā' in both states here. The meaning: they cannot rescue me from that harm. ﴿Indeed I would then be in clear error﴾: Nafi' and Abu 'Amr opened (fatḥah) this yā'.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed I have believed in your Lord﴾: Ahl al-Hijaz and Abu 'Amr opened this yā'.

Regarding whom he addressed with his faith, there are two opinions. One: he addressed his people with that; this was said by Ibn Mas'ud. The second: he addressed the messengers.

The meaning of ﴿so listen to me﴾ is: bear witness for me in this, as said by al-Farra'. Abu 'Ubaydah said: the meaning is: so listen to me. Ya'qub affirmed the yā' in "fasma'ūnī" in both states. Ibn Mas'ud said: when he addressed his people with that, they trampled him with their feet. al-Suddi said: they pelted him with stones while he was saying: "O Allah, guide my people."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿It was said: Enter Paradise﴾. When they killed him and he met Allah, it was said to him: "Enter Paradise." (p-14) When he entered it, ﴿he said: Would that my people knew﴾ ﴿of how my Lord has forgiven me﴾. Regarding "mā" there are two opinions.

One: it, together with "ghafara" (forgave), is in the position of a verbal noun; the meaning is: by the forgiveness of Allah to me.

The second: it means "alladhī" (that which); the meaning is: would that they knew of that by which my Lord forgave me, so that they would believe. Thus he advised them while alive and dead.

When they killed him, Allah hastened the punishment upon them. This is His saying: ﴿And We did not send down upon his people﴾, meaning the people of Habib, ﴿after him﴾, that is, after his killing, ﴿any host from the heaven﴾, meaning the angels; that is, He did not take vengeance upon them with a host from the heaven. ﴿Nor was it [Our practice] that We would send them down﴾ upon nations when We destroy them. It was also said: the meaning is: We did not send after him any prophet to them, nor did We send down to them any message.

﴿It was but one shout﴾. The commentators said: Jibril (Gabriel), peace be upon him, took hold of the two posts of the gate of the town, then shouted at them one shout, and behold, they were dead, with no sound heard from them, like a fire when it is extinguished. This is His saying: ﴿and behold, they were extinguished﴾, meaning: still, like the state of extinguished ashes.

(p. 15) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Alas for the servants!﴾ Al-Farrā' said: The meaning is, "How great is this regret over the servants!" Al-Zajjāj said: Ḥasrah (regret) is that a person experiences from intense remorse something without end, until his heart is left exhausted (ḥasīr). Regarding who is the one who regrets over the servants, there are two views.

The first: They regret over themselves. Mujāhid and al-Zajjāj said: Their mockery of the Messengers became a source of regret for them in the Hereafter. Abū al-'Āliyah said: When they witnessed the punishment, they said, "Alas for our regret over the Messengers! How can we have them now, so that we may believe?"

The second: The angels regret over the servants for their denial of the Messengers. This was said by al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

Then He warned the disbelievers of Makkah, saying: ﴿Have they not seen﴾, that is, have they not known, ﴿how many generations We destroyed before them﴾, so that they might take warning and fear that We might hasten their destruction as We hastened it for those We destroyed before them, and they would not return to the world? Al-Farrā' said: The alif of "annahum" is fatḥah (open), because the meaning is: "Have they not seen that they will not return to them?" Al-Ḥasan read it with kasrah (kasr), as if he did not make the seeing (ru'yah) govern "kam," so he did not make it govern "anna." If one begins a new clause after it, one reads it with kasrah.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And all of them, all of them﴾. The reading of 'Āṣim, Ibn 'Āmir, and Ḥamzah is "lammā" with tashdīd (shaddah): ﴿are brought before Us.﴾ That is, the nations will be brought forth on the Day of Resurrection and recompensed for their deeds. Al-Zajjāj said: Whoever reads "lamā" with takhfīf (lightening), then "mā" is a superfluous emphatic particle (zā'idah mu'akkidah), and the meaning is "Indeed, all of them are ..." and its meaning is: "All of them are only ones who will be brought before Us." Whoever reads "lammā" with tashdīd, it has the meaning of "illā" (except). You say: "I asked you 'lamā fa'alta' (i.e., 'except that you did')" and "illā fa'alta."

(p. 16) ﴿And a sign for them is the dead earth.﴾ Nāfi' read "al-mayyitah" with tashdīd, which is the original form, while takhfīf is more common, and both are permissible. "Āyah" is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is "lahum." It is also permissible for its predicate to be "al-arḍ al-mayyitah." The meaning is: a sign that indicates to them the Oneness of God and that God resurrects the dead, bringing to life the dead earth.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿from it they eat﴾, meaning what is eaten as food from the grains.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We placed in it﴾ and His saying ﴿and We caused springs to gush forth in it﴾, meaning in the earth.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿that they may eat of its fruit﴾, meaning the date palms, and it is masculine in form (lafẓ).

﴿and what their hands made﴾. Ibn Kathīr, Nāfi', Abū 'Amr, Ibn 'Āmir, and Ḥafṣ from 'Āṣim read "'amilat-hu" with the hā' (pronoun). Ḥamzah, al-Kisā'ī, and Abū Bakr from 'Āṣim read "'amilat" without the hā'. The hā' is written in the codices of Makkah, Madinah, Syria, and Basra, and omitted in the codices of the people of Kufa. Al-Zajjāj said: The position of "mā" is in the genitive (khafḍ); the meaning is: "that they may eat of its fruit and of what their hands made." It is also permissible for "mā" to be negative (nafy), meaning: "and their hands did not make it." This is according to the reading of those who affirm the hā'. Whoever reads "lammā" with tashdīd, it has the meaning of "illā" (except). You say: "I asked you 'lamā fa'alta' (i.e., 'except that you did')" and "illā fa'alta."

(p. 16) ﴿And a sign for them is the dead earth.﴾ Nāfi' read "al-mayyitah" with tashdīd, which is the original form, while takhfīf is more common, and both are permissible. "Āyah" is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is "lahum." It is also permissible for its predicate to be "al-arḍ al-mayyitah." The meaning is: a sign that indicates to them the Oneness of God and that God resurrects the dead, bringing to life the dead earth.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿from it they eat﴾, meaning what is eaten as food from the grains.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We placed in it﴾ and His saying ﴿and We caused springs to gush forth in it﴾, meaning in the earth.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿that they may eat of its fruit﴾, meaning the date palms, and it is masculine in form (lafẓ).

﴿and what their hands made﴾. Ibn Kathīr, Nāfi', Abū 'Amr, Ibn 'Āmir, and Ḥafṣ from 'Āṣim read "'amilat-hu" with the hā' (pronoun). Ḥamzah, al-Kisā'ī, and Abū Bakr from 'Āṣim read "'amilat" without the hā'. The hā' is written in the codices of Makkah, Madinah, Syria, and Basra, and omitted in the codices of the people of Kufa. Al-Zajjāj said: The position of "mā" is in the genitive (khafḍ); the meaning is: "that they may eat of its fruit and of what their hands made." It is also permissible for "mā" to be negative (nafy), meaning: "and their hands did not make it." This is according to the reading of those who affirm the hā'. When the hā' is omitted, the preferred view is that "mā" is in the genitive position and has the meaning of "alladhī" (which), so the omission of the hā' is good. Likewise, the exegetes mentioned both views. Whoever holds the first view says: "that they may eat of what their hands made," which is the planting and tilling in which they toiled. Whoever holds the second view says: "that they may eat what is not of their making, but it is from the act of the Truth, mighty and majestic." ﴿Will they not then be grateful?﴾ to God, the Exalted, so that they would affirm His Oneness?

Then He declared Himself exalted by His saying: ﴿Glory be to Him who created all the pairs﴾, meaning all the kinds, ﴿of what the earth grows﴾, of fruits, grains, and other things.

(p. 17) ﴿and of themselves﴾, that is, the males and females, ﴿and of what they do not know﴾, of the beasts of the land and the sea and other things that they have not come to know.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 36, verse 37–40:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And a sign for them is the night; We strip from it the day﴾, meaning: and a sign for them that points to Our oneness and Our power is the night; We strip from it the day. Al-Farra' said: "We cast the day off from it," and "min" (from) here means "'an" (from). Abu 'Ubayda said: "We bring out the day from it and separate it from it, so the darkness comes." Al-Mawardi said: "That is because the light of day mingles into the air and illuminates it; when it leaves, it grows dark." His saying: ﴿Then they are in darkness﴾, meaning: they enter into the dark.

﴿And the sun﴾, meaning: and a sign for them is the sun ﴿runs on to a resting place for it﴾. Concerning this there are four opinions.

The first: to the place of its settling. Abu Dharr reported: "I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about His saying: ﴿to a resting place for it﴾, and he said: 'Its resting place is beneath the Throne,' and he said: 'It goes on until it prostrates before its Lord, then it asks permission to rise, and permission is granted to it.'"

The second: its resting place is its setting point, which it does not pass beyond nor fall short of. This was said by Mujahid.

The third: for a single fixed time which it does not exceed. This was said by Qatadah. Muqatil said: for a time for it until the Day of Resurrection.

The fourth: it travels through its stations until it reaches its resting place, beyond which it does not go, then it returns to the first of its stations. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib. Ibn Qutaybah said: "To a resting place for it; its resting place is the farthest of its stations at setting, because it keeps advancing to the farthest of its western points, then it returns."

Ibn Mas'ud, 'Ikrimah, 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, and al-Shayzari from al-Kisa'i recited: "There is no resting place for it" (لا مُسْتَقَرَّ لَها), and the meaning is that it runs perpetually and never stays in one place.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That is the decree of the Almighty﴾, meaning: that which was mentioned of the matter of the night, the day and the sun, ﴿the decree of the Almighty﴾ in His dominion, ﴿the All-Knowing﴾ of what He decrees.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the moon﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr recited: "wal-qamaru" (والقَمَرُ) with a nominative ending. 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited: "wal-qamara" (والقَمَرَ) with an accusative ending. Al-Zajjaj said: whoever recites it in the accusative, the meaning is: "We decreed the moon, We decreed it as stations"; and whoever recites it in the nominative, the meaning is: "And a sign for them is the moon; We have decreed it," and it is permissible that it be in the nominative as a subject (mubtada'), with "We have decreed it" as the predicate (khabar).

The exegetes said: the stations of the moon are twenty-eight stations, which it passes through from the beginning of the month to its end. We have named them in Surah [Yunus: 5]. When it reaches the last of its stations, it becomes thin and returns like the old 'urjun, which is the stalk of the palm cluster left after the fruit stalks have been removed; when it dries out and becomes old, it resembles the crescent. Ibn Qutaybah said: "The old (qadim) here is that which a year has passed over, resembling the moon on the last night when it rises." Al-Zajjaj said: the form of "'urjun" is fa'lawn, from al-in'iraj.

Abu Mijlaz, Abu Raja', al-Dahhak, 'Asim al-Jahdari, and Ibn al-Sumayfa' recited: "ka-l-'irjun" (كالعُرْجُونِ) with a kasra on the 'ayn.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It is not for the sun to overtake the moon﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions.

The first: when they meet in the sky, one of them is before the other, so they do not share the stations. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: the light of one does not resemble the light of the other. This was said by Mujahid.

The third: the light of one does not join with the light of the other; when the authority of one comes, the authority of the other departs. This was said by Qatadah. The wisdom in this is that if the light were continuous, the night would not be recognized.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Nor does the night outstrip the day﴾. Abu al-Mutawakkil, Abu al-Jawza', Abu 'Imran, and 'Asim al-Jahdari recited: "sabiqun" (سابِقٌ) with tanwin and "al-nahara" (النَّهارَ) with an accusative ending. Concerning this there are two opinions.

The first: the night does not precede before the day is completed.

The second: no night comes after another night without a day separating them. The rest of the verse is explained in Surah [al-Anbiya': 33].

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿وَآيَةٌ لَهم أنّا حَمَلْنا ذُرِّيَّتَهُمْ﴾ قَرَأ نافِعٌ، وابْنُ عامِرٍ: "ذُرِّيّاتِهِمْ" عَلى الجَمْعِ؛ وقَرَأ الباقُونَ مِنَ السَّبْعَةِ (al-Sab'a, the seven canonical readers): "ذُرِّيَّتَهُمْ" عَلى التَّوْحِيدِ. قالَ المُفَسِّرُونَ: أرادَ: في سَفِينَةِ نُوحٍ، فَنَسَبَ الذُّرِّيَّةَ إلى المُخاطَبِينَ لِأنَّهم مِن جِنْسِهِمْ، كَأنَّهُ قالَ: ذُرِّيَّةُ النّاسِ. وقالَ الفَرّاءُ: أيْ: ذُرِّيَّةُ مَن هو مِنهُمْ، فَجَعَلَها ذَرِّيَّةً لَهُمْ، وقَدْ سَبَقَتْهم. وقالَ غَيْرُهُ: هو حَمْلُ الأنْبِياءِ في أصْلابِ الآَباءِ حِينَ رَكِبُوا السَّفِينَةَ، ومِنهُ قَوْلُ العَبّاسِ:

﴿بَلْ نُطْفَةٌ تَرْكَبُ السَّفِينَ وقَدْ ألْجَمَ نَسْرًا وأهْلَهُ الغَرَقُ﴾

قالَ المُفَضَّلُ بْنُ سَلَمَةَ: الذَّرِّيَّةُ: النَّسْلُ، لِأنَّهم مَن ذَرَأهُمُ اللَّهُ مِنهُمْ، والذُّرِّيَّةُ (p-٢٢) أيْضًا: الآَباءُ، لِأنَّ الذَّرَّ وقْعَ مِنهُمْ، فَهو مِنَ الأضْدادِ (al-addad, words that carry two opposite meanings)، ومِنهُ هَذِهِ الآَيَةُ، وقَدْ شَرَحْنا هَذا في قَوْلِهِ: ﴿ذُرِّيَّةً بَعْضُها مِن بَعْضٍ﴾ [آَلِ عِمْرانَ: ٣٤]؛ والمَشْحُونُ: المَمْلُوءُ.

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿وَخَلَقْنا لَهم مِن مِثْلِهِ﴾ فِيهِ قَوْلانِ.

أحَدُها: "ما بَيْنَ أيْدِيكُمْ": ما مَضى مِنَ الذُّنُوبِ، "وَما خَلْفَكُمْ": ما يَأْتِي مِنَ الذُّنُوبِ، قالَهُ مُجاهِدٌ.

(p-٢٣) والثّانِي: ["ما بَيْنَ أيْدِكُمْ"] ما تَقَدَّمَ مِن عَذابِ اللَّهِ لِلْأُمَمِ، "وَما خَلَفْكُمْ" مِن أمْرِ السّاعَةِ، قالَهُ قَتادَةُ.

والثّالِثُ: "ما بَيْنَ أيْدِيكُمْ" مِنَ الدُّنْيا، "وَما خَلْفَكُمْ" مِن عَذابِ الآَخِرَةِ. قالَهُ سُفْيانُ.

والرّابِعُ: "ما بَيْنَ أيْدِيكُمْ" مِن أمْرِ الآَخِرَةِ، "وَما خَلْفَكُمْ" مِن أمْرِ الدُّنْيا فَلا تَغْتَرُّوا بِها، قالَهُ ابْنُ عَبّاسٍ والكَلْبِيُّ.

﴿لَعَلَّكم تُرْحَمُونَ﴾ أيْ: لِتَكُونُوا عَلى رَجاءِ الرَّحْمَةِ مِنَ اللَّهِ. وجَوابُ "إذا" مَحْذُوفٌ، تَقْدِيرُهُ: إذا قِيلَ لَهم هَذا، أعْرَضُوا؛ ويَدُلُّ عَلى هَذا المَحْذُوفِ قَوْلُهُ: ﴿وَما تَأْتِيهِمْ مِن آيَةٍ﴾ أيْ: مِن دَلالَةٍ تَدُلُّ عَلى صِدْقِ الرَّسُولِ.

[p-24] His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Spend from what Allah has provided you"﴾. The commentators differed about who this verse was revealed concerning, in three views. The first: it concerns the Jews, related by al-Hasan. The second: it concerns the zanadiqa (heretics), related by Qatadah. The third: it concerns the polytheists of Quraysh, related by Muqatil. The reason is that the believers said to the disbelievers of Makkah: "Spend on the needy from the share that you claim belongs to Allah from the crops and livestock." They replied: ﴿Shall we feed one whom, if Allah willed, He would feed?﴾ Ibn al-Sa'ib said: when a needy person asked al-As ibn Wa'il, he would say, "Go to your Lord, for He is more fitting to you than I," and he would say, "Allah has withheld from him; shall I feed him?" The meaning of their words is that they said: "If Allah had willed to provide for them, He would have provided for them, so we agree with the will of Allah concerning them and do not feed them." This is an error on their part, because Allah Exalted made some of creation rich and some poor, in order to test the rich through the poor regarding what He has enjoined upon him in his wealth of zakat (obligatory alms). The believer does not object to the divine will; rather, he complies with the command. It has also been said that they only said this mockingly.

Regarding His saying: ﴿You are only in clear error﴾, there are two views. One: it is from the words of the disbelievers to the believers, meaning, "You are in error in following Muhammad." Two: it is from the words of Allah to the disbelievers, when they rejected it from the believers' side.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿When is this promise?﴾ They mean the Resurrection; the meaning is: when is the fulfilment of this promise? ﴿If you are truthful?﴾ They mean Muhammad and his companions.

﴿They await nothing﴾, i.e., they do not wait for anything ﴿but one Blast﴾, which is the first blast (al-nafkhah al-ula). The word ﴿yakhissimun﴾ means yakhtassun (they dispute), and the ta' was assimilated into the sad. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read "yakhsimun" with a fatha on the ya' and kha' and a shadda on the sad. It is related from Abu 'Amr that he weakly pronounced (ikhtilas) the vowel of the kha'. 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i read [p-25] "yakhiss̱imūn" with a fatha on the ya' and a kasra on the kha'. From 'Asim also: a kasra on both the ya' and the kha'. Nafi' read with a sukun on the kha' and a shadda on the sad. Hamzah read with a sukun on the kha' and a lightened sad, meaning yakhsimu ba'duhum ba'dan (some of them dispute with others). Ubayy ibn Ka'b read "yakhtasimun" with an added ta'. The meaning is that the Hour will come upon them while they are most heedless of it and busy with their transactions, buying and selling. ﴿So they will not be able to make a bequest﴾. Muqatil said: they were hurried away before making a will, and so they died. ﴿Nor will they return to their families﴾, i.e., they will not return from the markets to their homes. This is the description of what befalls them at the first blast. Then He mentioned what befalls them at the second blast, saying: ﴿And the Horn will be blown, and behold, they will rush from the graves﴾, meaning the graves, ﴿to their Lord﴾ ﴿yansilun﴾, i.e., they will emerge swiftly. We have explained this meaning in the chapter of al-Anbiya' [21:96].

﴿They will say: "Woe to us! Who has raised us from our resting place?"﴾ 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Abu Razin, al-Dahhak and 'Asim al-Jahdari read "min ba'thina" with a kasra on the mim and the tha' and a sukun on the 'ayn. The commentators said: they only said this because Allah Exalted lifted the punishment from them between the two blasts. Ubayy ibn Ka'b said: they will sleep a sleep before the resurrection, and when they are resurrected, they will say this.

[p-26] His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿This is what the Most Merciful promised﴾. Regarding the speakers of these words there are three views.

One: it is the words of the believers, related by Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Abi Layla. Qatadah said: the beginning of the verse is for the disbelievers, and its end is for the believers.

Two: it is the words of the angels to them, related by al-Hasan.

Three: it is the words of the disbelievers, who say to one another: "This is what the messengers told us, that we would be resurrected and recompensed," related by Ibn Zayd.

al-Zajjaj said: "min marqadina" is a pause of completion (waqf al-tamam). It is permissible that "hadha" is an attribute of "marqadina," with the meaning: "Who raised us from our resting place, this in which we were sleeping?" And in His saying "ma wa'ada al-Rahman" there is one of two implied words: either "hadha" or "haqq," so the meaning becomes: "True is what the Most Merciful promised."

[p-27] Then He mentioned the second blast, saying: ﴿It will be but one Blast﴾, and what follows is clear, up to His saying: ﴿Indeed, the companions of Paradise today﴾, meaning in the Hereafter, ﴿are busy in [a state of] occupation﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read "fi shughlin" with a sukun on the ghayn. 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "fi shughulin" with a damma on the shin and the ghayn. Abu Hurayrah, Abu Raja' and Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani read "fi shaghalin" with a fatha on the shin and the ghayn. Abu Mijlaz, Abu al-'Aliyah, 'Ikrimah, al-Dahhak, al-Nakha'i, Ibn Ya'mur and al-Jahdari read "fi shaghlin" with a fatha on the shin and a sukun on the ghayn. There are three views on its meaning.

One: their occupation is deflowering virgins. This was related by Shaqiq from Ibn Mas'ud, and by Mujahid from Ibn 'Abbas, and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, Qatadah and al-Dahhak also said this.

Two: the striking of lutes (al-awtar), related by 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas. It is also reported from 'Ikrimah as the two previous views; but this view is not authentic.

Three: enjoyment (al-ni'mah), said by Mujahid. al-Hasan said: their occupation is their bliss, distracting them from what the people of the Fire are in of punishment.

[p-28] His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Fakihun﴾ (enjoying fruits). Ibn Mas'ud, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, Abu al-Mutawakkil, Qatadah, Abu al-Jawza', al-Nakha'i and Abu Ja'far read "fakihun" (fakihun/fakihun variant as "fakihun" without alif). Is there a difference between them? There are two views.

As for "fakihun" (without alif), there are two views. One: that the fakih is one who enjoys (yatafakkahu), as the Arabs say of a man who enjoys food, fruit, or people's reputations: "Verily Fulan is fakih with such-and-such," and from it is said "fukahah" for jesting; this was said by Abu 'Ubaydah. Two: that "fakihin" means "farihin" (joyful), said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

The second view: "fakihun" and "fakihun" have the same meaning, as one says "hadhir" and "hadhir" (wary), said by al-Farra'. al-Zajjaj said: "fakihun" and "fakihun" mean "farihin" (joyful). Abu Zayd said: al-fakih is the one of good spirit, cheerful; one says "rajul fakih" and "fakih."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They and their spouses﴾, meaning their wives, ﴿in shade﴾. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read "fi zulalin" (with "zulal" as in "zulal"). al-Farra' said: "zilal" is the plural of "zill," and "zulal" is the plural of "zullah," though "zilal" may also be the plural of "zullah," as one says "khullah" and "khulal." When they are numerous they are "khilal," "khalal," and "qilal." Muqatil said: "zilal" are the shelters of palaces.

[p-29] Abu 'Ubaydah said: the meaning is that they are not exposed to the sun. As for "al-ara'ik" (couches), we have explained them in the chapter of al-Kahf [18:31].

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And for them is whatever they call for﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: "what they wish for." Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy ibn Ka'b and al-Jahdari read "salaman qawlan" with both in the accusative.

One: that the fakih is one who enjoys (yatafakkahu), as the Arabs say of a man who enjoys food, fruit, or people's reputations: "Verily Fulan is fakih with such-and-such," and from it is said "fukahah" for jesting; this was said by Abu 'Ubaydah. (p-30) Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And separate yourselves today, you guilty ones.﴾ Ibn Qutayba said: That is, withdraw from the believers and separate yourselves from them. It is said: "I separated (*mizt*) the thing from the thing" when you isolate it from it; so it becomes separated (*infaza*) and separates itself (*imtaza*), and "I separated it" (*mayyaztuhu*) so it becomes separated (*tamayyaza*).

The exegetes (*al-mufassirun*, those who write tafsir, the explanation of the Qur'an) said: When the humans and the jinn are mixed together in the Hereafter, it will be said: ﴿And separate yourselves today, you guilty ones.﴾ Then it will be said to the guilty: ﴿Did I not charge you﴾? That is: Did I not command you, did I not enjoin you? ﴿...that you should not worship Satan﴾. "Worship" (*ta'budu*) here means "obey" (*tuti'u*). Satan is Iblis, who adorned polytheism (*shirk*) for them, and they obeyed him. ﴿Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy﴾, evident in enmity, who removed your two parents from the Garden.

﴿And that worship Me﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, and al-Kisa'i read *"wa-an u'budūnī"* with a *ḍamma* on the *nūn*. 'Asim, Abu 'Amr, and Hamza read *"wa-an u'budūnī"* with a *kasra* on the *nūn*. The meaning is: Affirm My oneness (*waḥḥidūnī*). ﴿This is a straight path﴾, meaning monotheism (*tawhid*).

﴿And he had already led astray from you a great number (*jibillan*)﴾. Ibn Kathir, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Khalaf read *"jabalan"* with a *ḍamma* on the *jīm* and the *bā'*, and a lightened *lām*. Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read *"jabalan"* with a *ḍamma* on the *jīm*, a sukun on the *bā'*, and a lightened *lām*. Nafi' and 'Asim read *"jibillan"* with a *kasra* on the *jīm* and the *bā'*, with a doubled *lām*. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn 'Abbas, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, al-Zuhri, and al-A'mash read *"jabbalan"* with a *ḍamma* on the *jīm* and the *bā'*, with a doubled *lām*. 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr and Ibn al-Sumayfa' read *"jibilan"* with a *kasra* on the *jīm*, a sukun on the *bā'*, and a lightened *lām*. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu al-Mutawakkil, and Mu'adh al-Qari' read *"jubalan"* with a *raf'* (*ḍamma*) on the *jīm*, a *fatḥa* on the *bā'*, and a lightened *lām*. So the meaning is: (p-31) "And he had already led astray from you a great creation (*khalqan kathīran*)." ﴿Did you not then understand?﴾ That is: You have seen the traces of those destroyed before you through obedience to Satan; did you not then understand this?

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 36, verses 65–68:**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Today We will seal their mouths﴾. Abu al-Mutawakkil and Abu al-Jawza' read "يَخْتِمُ" (*yakhtimu*) with a dammed *yā'* and a fatha on the *tā'*. Ibn Mas'ud read "وَلِتُكَلِّمُنا" (*wa-li-tukallimunā*) with an added kasra-ed *lām*, a fatha on the *mīm*, and a *wāw* before the *lām*. Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ibn Abi 'Abla read "لِتُكَلِّمُنا" (*li-tukallimunā*) with a kasra-ed *lām*, without a *wāw* before it, and with a fatha on the *mīm*. All of them read "وَلِتَشْهَدَ أرْجُلُهُمْ" (*wa-li-tashhada arjuluhum*) with a kasra-ed *lām* and a fatha on the *dāl*.

The meaning of "نَخْتِمُ" (*nakhtimu*) is: We will stamp upon them. It was said that preventing them from speaking is the sealing upon them. Regarding the cause of this, there are four opinions.

The first: when they said, ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ (Al-An'am 6:23), Allah sealed their mouths and their limbs spoke. This was said by Abu Musa al-Ash'ari.

The second: so that they would know that their limbs, which had been helpers to them in disobedience, had become witnesses [against them].

(p. 32) The third: so that the people of the place of standing would recognize them and distinguish them by this.

The fourth: because the testimony of the limbs is more eloquent in confession than the speech of the tongue. Al-Mawardi mentioned these.

If it is asked: what is the wisdom in calling the speech of the hand "speech" (kalam) and the speech of the foot "testimony" (shahada)?

The answer: the hand was the one directly engaged in the act, while the foot was present. The statement of one who is present about another is testimony to what he saw, while the statement of the doer against himself is confession of what he did.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And if We willed, We would have obliterated their eyes﴾. Regarding this there are three opinions.

The first: "And if We willed, We would have removed their eyes entirely, so that no slit or eyelid would appear for them." The one whose eyes are obliterated is the one who has no slit between his eyelids. ﴿So they would race to the path﴾, i.e., they would hasten to the way. ﴿Then how would they see?﴾ [i.e.]: how would they see when We have blinded their eyes? Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr, and Abu Raja' read "فاسْتَبْقَوْا" (*fa-istabaqū*) with a kasra on the *bā'*, and "فَأنّى تُبْصِرُونَ" (*fa-anna tubṣirūn*) with a *tā'*. This is a threat to the people of Makkah, and it is the view of the majority.

The second: "And if We willed, We would have led them astray and blinded them from guidance, so how would they see the truth?" Ibn Abi Talha narrated this from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: "And if We willed, We would have gouged out the eyes of their misguidance, blinded them from their error, and turned their sights from misguidance to guidance so that they would see their right path. So how would they see, when I have not done that to them?" This was narrated from a group of them, including Muqatil.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And if We willed, We would have transformed them in their places﴾. Abu Bakr narrated from 'Asim: "عَلى مَكاناتِهِمْ" (*ʿalā makānātihim*). The explanation of this has already passed (Al-Baqara 2:65).

(p. 33) Regarding the meaning of His saying ﴿We would have transformed them﴾ (*la-maskhnāhum*) there are four opinions. The first: We would have destroyed them; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: We would have made them sit upon their feet; this was said by al-Hasan and Qatada. The third: We would have made them stones; this was said by Abu Salih and Muqatil. The fourth: We would have made them monkeys and swine without spirits in them; this was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

Regarding His saying: ﴿So they would not be able to go forward or return﴾ there are three opinions. The first: they would not be able to advance or to retreat; this was said by Qatada. The second: they would not be able to go forward away from the punishment, nor return to their original form after the transformation; this was said by al-Dahhak. The third: they would not be able to go forward out of the world, nor return to it; this was said by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And whomever We grant long life, We reverse him in creation﴾. Hamza read "نُنَكِّسُهُ" (*nunakkisuhu*) with a shadda, with a damma on the first *nūn* and a fatha on the second. The rest read it with a fatha on the first *nūn* and a sukun on the second, without a shadda; and from 'Asim there are two readings like these. The meaning of the statement is: whoever We prolong his life, We reverse his creation, so We put weakness in place of strength and senility in place of youth, and We return him to the lowest age. ﴿Will they not then use their reason?﴾ Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read "أفَلا تَعْقِلُونَ" (*afalā taʿqilūn*) with a *tā'*; the rest read it with a *yā'*. The meaning is: will they not reason that the One who did this is able to resurrect?

All of them read "وَلِتَشْهَدَ أرْجُلُهُمْ" (*wa-li-tashhada arjuluhum*) with a kasra-ed *lām* and a fatha on the *dāl*.

The meaning of "نَخْتِمُ" (*nakhtimu*) is: We will stamp upon them. It was said that preventing them from speaking is the sealing upon them. Regarding the cause of this, there are four opinions.

The first: when they said, ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ (Al-An'am 6:23), Allah sealed their mouths and their limbs spoke. This was said by Abu Musa al-Ash'ari.

The second: so that they would know that their limbs, which had been helpers to them in disobedience, had become witnesses [against them].

(p. 32) The third: so that the people of the place of standing would recognize them and distinguish them by this.

The fourth: because the testimony of the limbs is more eloquent in confession than the speech of the tongue. Al-Mawardi mentioned these.

If it is asked: what is the wisdom in calling the speech of the hand "speech" (kalam) and the speech of the foot "testimony" (shahada)?

The answer: the hand was the one directly engaged in the act, while the foot was present. The statement of one who is present about another is testimony to what he saw, while the statement of the doer against himself is confession of what he did.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And if We willed, We would have obliterated their eyes﴾. Regarding this there are three opinions.

The first: "And if We willed, We would have removed their eyes entirely, so that no slit or eyelid would appear for them." The one whose eyes are obliterated is the one who has no slit between his eyelids. ﴿So they would race to the path﴾, i.e., they would hasten to the way. ﴿Then how would they see?﴾ [i.e.]: how would they see when We have blinded their eyes? Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr, and Abu Raja' read "فاسْتَبْقَوْا" (*fa-istabaqū*) with a kasra on the *bā'*, and "فَأنّى تُبْصِرُونَ" (*fa-anna tubṣirūn*) with a *tā'*. This is a threat to the people of Makkah, and it is the view of the majority.

The second: "And if We willed, We would have led them astray and blinded them from guidance, so how would they see the truth?" Ibn Abi Talha narrated this from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: "And if We willed, We would have gouged out the eyes of their misguidance, blinded them from their error, and turned their sights from misguidance to guidance so that they would see their right path. So how would they see, when I have not done that to them?" This was narrated from a group of them, including Muqatil.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And if We willed, We would have transformed them in their places﴾. Abu Bakr narrated from 'Asim: "عَلى مَكاناتِهِمْ" (*ʿalā makānātihim*). The explanation of this has already passed (Al-Baqara 2:65).

(p. 33) Regarding the meaning of His saying ﴿We would have transformed them﴾ (*la-maskhnāhum*) there are four opinions. The first: We would have destroyed them; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: We would have made them sit upon their feet; this was said by al-Hasan and Qatada. The third: We would have made them stones; this was said by Abu Salih and Muqatil. The fourth: We would have made them monkeys and swine without spirits in them; this was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

Regarding His saying: ﴿So they would not be able to go forward or return﴾ there are three opinions. The first: they would not be able to advance or to retreat; this was said by Qatada. The second: they would not be able to go forward away from the punishment, nor return to their original form after the transformation; this was said by al-Dahhak. The third: they would not be able to go forward out of the world, nor return to it; this was said by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And whomever We grant long life, We reverse him in creation﴾. Hamza read "نُنَكِّسُهُ" (*nunakkisuhu*) with a shadda, with a damma on the first *nūn* and a fatha on the second. The rest read it with a fatha on the first *nūn* and a sukun on the second, without a shadda; and from 'Asim there are two readings like these. The meaning of the statement is: whoever We prolong his life, We reverse his creation, so We put weakness in place of strength and senility in place of youth, and We return him to the lowest age. ﴿Will they not then use their reason?﴾ Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read "أفَلا تَعْقِلُونَ" (*afalā taʿqilūn*) with a *tā'*; the rest read it with a *yā'*. The meaning is: will they not reason that the One who did this is able to resurrect?

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 36, verses 69–70:

Allah's words: ﴿And We did not teach him poetry, nor is it fitting for him.﴾ The exegetes (mufassirun) said: The disbelievers of Makkah said, "This Qur'an is poetry, and Muhammad is a poet." So Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We did not teach him poetry, nor is it fitting for him.﴾ That is, it would not be easy for him to do so. The exegetes said: No line of poetry would balance properly for him. It is narrated from him ﷺ that one day he recited (tamaththala) and said:

"Islam and grey hair are sufficient for a man as a restrainer."

Abu Bakr said: "O Messenger of Allah, he only said:

*Grey hair and Islam are sufficient for a man as a restrainer.*

I bear witness that you are the Messenger of Allah. Allah did not teach you poetry, nor is it fitting for you."

And one day he called ʿAbbas ibn Mirdas and said, "You are the one who said:

*Shall you make my plunder and the plunder of the slaves divided between al-Aqra' and ʿUyayna?*"

Abu Bakr said: "May my father and mother be your ransom, he did not say it like that." So Abu Bakr recited it (the correct version), and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "It does not harm you which of the two you began with." Abu Bakr said: "By Allah, you are not a poet, and poetry is not fitting for you."

And one day he recited, saying:

*"And there comes to you one whom you have not provisioned with news."*

Abu Bakr said: "It is not like this, O Messenger of Allah." So he said: "Indeed I am not a poet, nor is it fitting for me."

He was prevented from composing poetry only so that doubt would not enter upon a people concerning what he brought of the Qur'an, and they would say: "He became capable of it through what is in his nature of keen intelligence for poetry."

Allah's words: ﴿It is not but a reminder﴾ meaning, the Qur'an, ﴿and a clear Qur'an﴾, that is, an admonition, ﴿in which are the obligations and the sunan (recommended practices) [and the rulings].﴾

Allah's words: ﴿That he may warn﴾. Ibn Kathir, ʿAsim, Abu ʿAmr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "liyunzira" with the *ya'* (third person), meaning the Qur'an. Nafi', Ibn ʿAmir and Yaʿqub read "litunzira" with the *ta'* (second person), meaning the Prophet ﷺ; that is, "that you may warn, O Muhammad, by what is in the Qur'an." Abu al-Mutawakkil, Abu al-Jawza' and Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ read "liyundhira" with a *ya'* marked with a *damma* and the *dhal* and *ra'* both with a *fatha*.

Allah's words: ﴿whoever is alive﴾. There are four opinions concerning it:

First: one whose heart is alive and whose sight is alive. This was said by Qatadah.

Second: whoever is intelligent. This was said by al-Dahhak. Al-Zajjaj said: whoever understands what he is addressed with, for the disbeliever is like the dead in regard to the warner's warning.

Third: one who is guided. This was said by al-Suddi. Muqatil said: whoever is guided in the knowledge of Allah.

Fourth: whoever is a believer. This was said by Yahya ibn Salam. This is according to the meaning that has already preceded in His words: ﴿You only warn those who fear their Lord﴾ [Fatir: 18]. It is also permissible that he means: your warning only benefits whoever is a believer in the knowledge of Allah.

Allah's words: ﴿and the word may be justified against the disbelievers﴾. Its meaning: it becomes obligatory (yajib). Concerning what is meant by "the word," there are two opinions. One: that it is the punishment. Two: that it is the proof (hujjah).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 36, verses 71–76:

Then He reminded them of His power, saying: ﴿Do they not see that We created for them, among what Our hands have made, livestock?﴾ Ibn Qutayba said: It is possible that the meaning is "among what We have made by Our strength and power." In the hand is power and ability to act, so the hand is used metaphorically and placed in its position. This is a figure of speech of the Arabs which this wording permits, and God knows best what He intended. Others said: The mention of the hands here indicates His sole creation of what He made. The meaning is that no one shared with Us in Our creating. When one of us says, "I made this with my hand," it indicates that he alone did the work. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: The meaning of the verse is "among what We brought into being by Our power and strength." This is a consensus (ijma') that He intended here nothing other than what we have mentioned.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they are its owners﴾ has two interpretations.

The first: they are those who control it. This was said by Qatada and Muqatil. Al-Zajjaj said: A similar usage in poetry is:

"I have become one who does not carry weapons, nor does he hold the head of a camel if it bolts."

That is, "I do not control the head of the camel."

The second: they are capable of dominating them through their subjugation for them. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We made them subservient to them﴾, that is, We subjected them, so they are docile to them. ﴿So some of them they ride﴾. Ibn Qutayba said: The rukub is what they ride, and the halub is what they milk. Al-Farra' said: If a reciter read "fa-minha ruku-buhum" (with a ḍamma on the rā'), it would be a valid reading, as you say: "From it is their eating, their drinking, and their riding." Al-Hasan, Abu al-'Aliya, al-A'mash, and Ibn Ya'mur, among others, read it with a ḍamma on the rā'. Ubayy ibn Ka'b and 'Aisha read "rakubatahum" with a fatha on the rā' and the bā', and with an added raised tā' (rakūbatahum, i.e., a fatḥa on the rā' and bā' with a final tā' marked as the nominative). The exegetes said: They ride the camels from among the livestock, and they eat the sheep. ﴿And for them in them are benefits﴾ from the wool, the fleece, the hair, and the offspring, ﴿and drinks﴾ [from] their milk. ﴿Will they not then be grateful?﴾ to the Lord of these blessings, so that they would affirm His oneness?

Then He mentioned their ignorance, saying: ﴿And they have taken besides God gods, that they might be helped﴾, that is, to protect them from the punishment of God. Then He informed that this would not happen, by His saying: ﴿They are unable to help them﴾, that is, the idols cannot prevent them from any matter that God intends for them. ﴿And they﴾, meaning the disbelievers, ﴿for them﴾, meaning the idols, ﴿are a host brought forth﴾. There are four opinions concerning this.

The first: they are a host in this world, brought forth in the Fire. This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: they are brought forth at the reckoning. This was said by Mujahid.

The third: the polytheists are a host for the idols; they become angry for them in this world, while the idols do not bring them any good nor repel any harm from them. This was said by Qatada. Muqatil said: The disbelievers become angry for the gods and attend them in this world. Al-Zajjaj said: They are, for the idols, those who give victory, while the idols cannot give them victory.

The fourth: they are a host brought forth before the idols, worshipping them. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So let not their speech grieve you﴾, meaning the speech of the disbelievers of Makkah in denying you. ﴿Indeed, We know what they conceal﴾ in their hearts of their denial of you, ﴿and what they reveal﴾ with their tongues of that. The meaning is: We will reward you and requite them.

**(p. 40)** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Does not man see that We created him from a drop of semen?﴾ The scholars differed over who this verse and the ones following it were revealed about, giving five opinions.

The first: it was al-'As ibn Wa'il al-Sahmi, who took a bone from the gravel-plain (al-Batha'), crumbled it in his hand, and said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Will Allah bring this back to life after it has rotted?" He said: "Yes. Allah will cause you to die, then bring you back to life, then cause you to enter the Fire of Jahannam." Then these verses were revealed. This was narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: it was 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, and a similar story happened to him. This was narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas.

**(p. 41)** The third: it was Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, and this story happened to him. This was narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas.

The fourth: it was Umayyah ibn Khalaf. This was said by al-Hasan.

The fifth: it was Ubayy ibn Khalaf al-Jumahi, and this story happened to him. This was said by Mujahid, Qatadah and the majority, and the exegetes (al-mufassirun) hold this view.

The meaning of the speech is an expression of wonder at the ignorance of this disputant in denying resurrection. The meaning is: Does he not know that he is a created being, so that he would reflect on the beginning of his creation and abandon his dispute? It has also been said: this is a reminder to him of Allah's blessing upon him, in that He brought him into being from a drop of semen, and yet he became a disputer.

﴿And he presents for Us a parable﴾: in denying resurrection, by means of the decayed bone when he crumbled it in his hand, and he wondered at the one who says that Allah will bring it back to life. ﴿And forgets his creation﴾: that is, he forgot Our creating him, i.e. **(p. 42)** he neglected to reflect upon the creation of himself, since he was created from a drop of semen. ﴿He says: "Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?"﴾ That is, when they are rotten. It is said: "ramma al-'azm" (ر م ّ العظم, "the bone rotted") when it decayed, so it is ﴿rameem﴾ (رَمِيمٌ). Because it is an altered form (ma'dul) from its doer (fa'il) and every altered form from its original pattern and measure is diverted from its i'rab (inflectional grammatical function, i.e. the case endings and grammatical status of the word), as in His saying: ﴿And your mother was not unchaste﴾ [Maryam: 28], where the ta' marbutah was dropped because the word is diverted from "baghiyah". So this disbeliever measured the power of Allah, exalted is He, by the power of the creatures, and so he denied the reviving of the decayed bone, because that is not within the capacity of creatures. ﴿Say: "He will give them life who brought them into being the first time"﴾, i.e. He initiated their creation, ﴿and He is Knower of every creation﴾, of both the beginning and the return. ﴿Knower﴾.

﴿He who made for you fire from the green tree﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: He meant the fire-sticks (al-zunud) with which the Bedouins kindle fire, from the trees of al-markh and al-'ifar.

If it is asked: Why did He say "al-shajar al-akhdar" (the green tree, singular adjective), and not "al-shajar al-khudr" (the green trees, plural adjective)?

The answer: "al-shajar" is a collective noun, and it may be treated as feminine or masculine. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then you will be filling your bellies from it﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 53], and He said: ﴿Then from it you kindle﴾.

Then He mentioned what is greater than the creation of man, and said: ﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able﴾. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq and 'Asim al-Jahdari read **"yaqdir"** (يَقْدِرُ) with a ya' and without an alif (ـا), ﴿to create the likes of them?﴾ This is an interrogation of affirmation (istifham taqrir), and the meaning is: he who was able to do that great thing is able to do this small thing. We have explained the meaning of "to create the likes of them" in [al-Isra': 99]. Then He answered this interrogation, saying: ﴿Yes, and He is the Creator (al-Khallaq)﴾, creating creation after creation. Ubayy ibn Ka'b, al-Hasan and 'Asim al-Jahdari read **"wa-Huwa al-Khaliq"** (وَهُوَ الخالِقُ). ﴿The Knower﴾ of all that is known.
